title.narrative: Chimbonde (re) settlement: Building resilience through inclusive, sustainable and durable solutions to disaster induced displacement in Tete, Mozambique

description.narrative:
DESCRIPTION Nearing the fourth anniversary of the landfall of Cyclone Idai in Mozambique, which brought widespread destruction in particular in the central region, the affected populations—who were already highly vulnerable from a socio-economic or climatic perspective—are still struggling to rebuild their disrupted lives. Despite having been relocated away from areas where they had been constantly exposed to disasters and having received support from the government as well as humanitarian and development partners, many of the pre-existing challenges persist. Recovery remains elusive, and sustainable and durable solutions to disaster-induced displacement are still far from being met. The unprecedented reconstruction effort, coordinated by the government and resulting in an ambitious reconstruction programme called PREPOC, is still largely underfunded. The effort has been made even more challenging by a series of successive disasters affecting the same area in the following years, including cyclone Eloise, tropical storms Chalane and Ana, and more recently, cyclones Gombe and Freddy. These disasters demonstrate the relevance of Mozambique pursuing climate resilience, building back better from disasters, and promoting adaptation across its communities. The province of Tete, one of the affected provinces in the Central Region, has received relatively limited support compared to Sofala province, where the majority of reconstruction operations and their funds are currently being implemented. However, the city of Tete can be considered a good example of how urban exposure to natural disasters and resulting internal displacement should be seen as an integrated dynamic. This dynamic links adaptation and disaster risk reduction mechanisms in the productive areas where communities build their livelihood, to the improved quality of life in the residential areas where they are resettled. It constitutes a fundamental element for sustainable and durable solutions to displacement, contributing to local socio-economic development.
Figure 1 - In blue the most vulnerable area of the city to floods Families living in the City of Tete's lowlands, at the junction of the Zambesi and Revubue rivers, were forced to flee their homes when floods caused by the cyclones earlier mentioned struck the area. As a result, they have been relocated by the government to the Chimbonde area, located in the north-west periphery of the city, with initial support from humanitarian actors such as IOM and UNHCR. However, the families are still facing a precarious situation in terms of service coverage, basic infrastructure, security of tenure, and housing. In Mozambique, the Regulation on the Resettlement Process Resulting from Economic Activities (Decree no. 31/2012, of 8 August) is in force, as is the Policy and Strategy for the Management of Internally Displaced Persons, as a result of (i) socio-economic (ii) natural and (iii) human factors. However, its application is flawed, particularly in the process of supervising and regulating aspects considered essential for assessing and monitoring compliance with the law, with a focus on the weak or no involvement of communities in making decisions about their lives. The legislation in force, with a focus on the mechanisms that guide the resettlement process, does not take into account the specificities in the social construction of male and female identities, nor the differentiation in the division of labour and access to rights. This situation results in a worsening of women's lives, both in terms of their economic autonomy (to some extent already affected in the areas of origin) and in terms of access to and defence of rights, such as the possibility of reporting domestic violence in the resettlement areas, where there are still no mechanisms in place to do so. The same happens when it comes to access to resources, which manifests itself, on the one hand, in the impossibility of reproducing her way of life as the provider of food for the family and in the reduction of her ability to achieve some economic autonomy, even if this must be perceived within the limits imposed by the power structure. In the context of disaster-induced displacement in Tete, as well as in several other areas of Mozambique, many families rely on agriculture as their primary source of income and livelihood. The lowlands provide fertile and humid soil that supports agricultural activities, fishery, and livestock. In many cases, the resettlement of these families to high and safer areas does not necessarily mean that they will not return to the productive areas for their agricultural activities, including the traditional structures called "casas de machamba" (farmhouses), especially during peak seasons for preparing fields or harvesting crops.
